title: Quiz 2 Gym
eyebrow: COMP9020 · Drill · Quiz 2 on Thu 1 Oct 2026
goal: Do the two Quiz 2 question types fast and without traps: match English statements to equivalent formulas, and pick every formula a premise entails.
magic: Translate first, then rewrite: `A ⇒ B = ¬A ∨ B`, `A ⇒ (B ⇒ C) = (A ∧ B) ⇒ C`.
Entailed = T in every premise-row. One F kills it.

blocks.title: Before you start: how the two Quiz 2 questions work
steps: **The quiz** (Week 2 slide 2, Problem set 2 footer): at the start of your tutorial, closed book, no devices. You get your own variation of **Q3(b)** and **Q5(b)**. 1 mark each, partial marks possible.

**Q3(b)-type:** two English statements, a list of formulas. Translate each statement FIRST (letters on paper), then rewrite with `A ⇒ B = ¬A ∨ B`, `A ⇒ (B ⇒ C) = (A ∧ B) ⇒ C`, De Morgan, and `¬A ⇔ B = A ⊕ B`. Match each option to one statement.
**Traps to check on every option:** "only if" never flips · "unless" = if not · "neither … nor" = `¬a ∧ ¬b` · a `¬` on one side of `⇔` turns it into `⊕` · one direction of `⇔` is not enough.
**Q5(b)-type:** one premise, several candidate formulas. Write the premise's true rows in a mini-table ONCE. A candidate is entailed exactly when it is T in **every** one of those rows.
**Speed tip:** a candidate that is the premise rewritten (contrapositive, `¬A ∨ B` form) is always entailed. A candidate that is F in one premise-row is out. Stop checking it at the first F.

blocks.title: Round 1 · English → pick the equivalent formulas
blocks.sub: Seven original scenarios in the exact shape of the quiz's Q3(b): two statements, five formulas.

items.q:
**S1:** "Provided the room is cold, the heater is on unless a window is open."
**S2:** "The heater is on only if no window is open."
Select the formulas that are logically equivalent to S1 or to S2.
items.why: S1 = `c ⇒ (¬w ⇒ h)` ("provided" marks the outer condition; "unless" = if not). Rewrite each `⇒` as `¬A ∨ B`: `¬c ∨ w ∨ h`, which is (4). S2 = `h ⇒ ¬w` = `¬h ∨ ¬w` = `¬(h ∧ w)`, which is (2). (1) wrongly forces `¬w` whenever it's cold. (3) says `h ⇔ w`. (5) is true whenever the heater is on, even with no cold room.
items.letters: `h` = the heater is on · `w` = a window is open · `c` = the room is cold
items.wrong: If you picked (1): "unless a window is open" doesn't promise the window is shut. It only says what happens when it's shut.

items.q:
**S1:** "We deploy only if the tests pass and the code is reviewed."
**S2:** "Whenever the tests fail, we don't deploy unless the code is reviewed."
Select the formulas that are logically equivalent to S1 or to S2.
items.why: S1 = `d ⇒ (t ∧ r)` = `¬d ∨ (t ∧ r)`, and distributing gives (3). S2 = `¬t ⇒ (¬r ⇒ ¬d)` = `t ∨ r ∨ ¬d`, which is (5). (1) is the converse of S1. (2) is `¬d ∨ t ∨ ¬r`, which has the wrong sign on `r`. (4) is exactly the situation that **breaks** S2.
items.letters: `t` = the tests pass · `r` = the code is reviewed · `d` = we deploy
items.wrong: If you picked (1): "only if" never flips. The deploy is on the left.

items.q:
**S1:** "The coffee machine brews exactly when it is switched on and has water."
**S2:** "It isn't switched on unless it has water."
Select the formulas that are logically equivalent to S1 or to S2.
items.why: S1 = `b ⇔ (o ∧ m)`: both directions. (2) spells out both: `b ⇒ o` and `b ⇒ m` together are `b ⇒ (o ∧ m)`, plus the way back. S2 = `¬m ⇒ ¬o` = `o ⇒ m` = `¬o ∨ m`, which is (4). (1) is the converse of S2. (3) is only one direction of S1. (5) doesn't match either.
items.letters: `b` = the machine brews · `o` = it is switched on · `m` = it has water
items.wrong: If you picked (3): "exactly when" is `⇔`. One direction isn't enough.

items.q:
**S1:** "You don't pay a late fee just in case the book is returned on time or the loan is extended."
**S2:** "The loan is extended only if the book isn't returned on time."
Select the formulas that are logically equivalent to S1 or to S2.
items.why: S1 = `¬l ⇔ (r ∨ x)`. "Not A just in case B" means A and B are **opposite**, and that is `⊕`: `l ⊕ (r ∨ x)`, which is (4). S2 = `x ⇒ ¬r` = `¬x ∨ ¬r` = `¬(x ∧ r)`, which is (5). (1) drops the "don't": it says the fee matches. (2) is the converse-style mix-up of S2. (3) allows `l` with `x` true.
items.letters: `l` = you pay a late fee · `r` = the book is returned on time · `x` = the loan is extended
items.wrong: If you picked (1): the `¬` on `l` matters. `¬l ⇔ Y` is the opposite of `l ⇔ Y`.

items.q:
**S1:** "Whenever the key is in the ignition, the alarm beeps unless the seatbelt is fastened."
**S2:** "The alarm beeps only if the key is in the ignition and the seatbelt isn't fastened."
Select the formulas that are logically equivalent to S1 or to S2.
items.why: S1 = `k ⇒ (¬s ⇒ a)`, and `A ⇒ (B ⇒ C)` = `(A ∧ B) ⇒ C`, which is (2). S2 = `a ⇒ (k ∧ ¬s)` = `¬a ∨ (k ∧ ¬s)`; distributing gives (4). (1) has `¬s` where S1 has `s` (`¬k ∨ s ∨ a`). (3) forgets the seatbelt. (5) is S1 and S2 together, stronger than either.
items.letters: `k` = the key is in the ignition · `s` = the seatbelt is fastened · `a` = the alarm beeps
items.wrong: If you picked (5): it is true exactly when S1 **and** S2 both hold. Each option should match ONE statement.

items.q:
**S1:** "Provided I don't take the car, I take an umbrella if it rains."
**S2:** "When it doesn't rain, I take neither the car nor an umbrella."
Select the formulas that are logically equivalent to S1 or to S2.
items.why: S1 = `¬c ⇒ (r ⇒ u)` = `(¬c ∧ r) ⇒ u`, which is (4). S2 = `¬r ⇒ (¬c ∧ ¬u)` = `r ∨ (¬c ∧ ¬u)`, which is (1). (3) says "not both", weaker than "neither". (5) flips the contrapositive the wrong way: S2's contrapositive is `(c ∨ u) ⇒ r`. (2) matches neither.
items.letters: `r` = it rains · `u` = I take an umbrella · `c` = I take the car
items.wrong: If you picked (3): "neither … nor" is `¬c ∧ ¬u`. "Not both" `¬(c ∧ u)` allows taking one of them.

items.q:
**S1:** "Requests error if and only if the server is down or the queue is full."
**S2:** "The queue is full only if the server is up."
Select the formulas that are logically equivalent to S1 or to S2.
items.why: S1 = `e ⇔ (¬u ∨ q)`. Negate both sides of a `⇔` and it stays true: `¬e ⇔ ¬(¬u ∨ q)` = `¬e ⇔ (u ∧ ¬q)`, which is (5). S2 = `q ⇒ u` = `¬q ∨ u`, which is (2). (1) and (4) are each only one direction of S1. (3) is the converse of S2.
items.letters: `e` = requests error · `u` = the server is up · `q` = the queue is full
items.wrong: If you picked (1): "if and only if" needs both directions. (1) alone allows errors to be missing when the server is down.

blocks.title: Round 2 · Which formulas are entailed?
blocks.sub: Eight original premises in the shape of the quiz's Q5(b).

items.q: Which are logically entailed by `(p ∨ q) ⇒ ¬r`?
items.why: Premise-rows (`p q r`): FFF, FFT, FTF, TFF, TTF. (1) `p ⇒ ¬r` ✅. (2) `r ⇒ ¬q` ✅ (the only `r = T` row is FFT). (3) `¬r` ❌ at FFT. (4) `¬p ∨ ¬q ∨ ¬r` ✅ (never all three T). (5) `(p ∧ q) ⇒ r` ❌ at TTF.

items.q: Which are logically entailed by `¬(p ⇔ q) ∧ (q ∨ r)`?
items.why: Premise-rows: FTF, FTT, TFT. (1) `p ∨ q` ✅. (2) `r` ❌ at FTF. (3) `p ⇒ r` ✅ (the only `p = T` row has `r = T`). (4) `q ⇒ ¬p` ✅. (5) `¬q ⇒ (p ∧ r)` ✅ (the only `q = F` row is TFT).

items.q: Which are logically entailed by `¬(x ⇒ y) ∨ z`?
items.why: Premise-rows (`x y z`): FFT, FTT, TFF, TFT, TTT. (1) `z` ❌ at TFF. (2) `x ∨ z` ✅. (3) `y ⇒ z` ✅ (every `y = T` row has `z = T`). (4) `¬y ∨ z` is (3) again ✅. (5) `(x ∧ ¬z) ⇒ ¬y` ✅ (the only `x = T, z = F` row has `y = F`).

items.q: Which are logically entailed by `p ∨ (q ∧ ¬r)`?
items.why: Premise-rows: the four `p = T` rows plus FTF. (1) `p ∨ q` ✅. (2) `¬r ⇒ p` ❌ at FTF. (3) `r ⇒ p` ✅ (FTF has `r = F`). (4) `q ∨ ¬r` ❌ at TFT. (5) `¬p ⇒ ¬r` ✅ (same as (3)).

items.q: Which are logically entailed by `¬(a ∨ (b ∧ c))`?
items.why: Premise-rows (`a b c`): FFF, FFT, FTF. (1) `¬a` ✅. (2) `¬b` ❌ at FTF. (3) `¬b ∨ ¬c` ✅. (4) `b ⇒ ¬c` is (3) again ✅. (5) `a ⇒ b` ✅ (`a` is always F).

items.q: Which are logically entailed by `(p ⊕ q) ⇒ r`?
items.why: Premise-rows: every row except TFF and FTF. (1) `r` ❌ at FFF. (2) `¬r ⇒ (p ⇔ q)` ✅ (it's the contrapositive). (3) `p ∨ q ∨ r` ❌ at FFF. (4) `(p ∧ ¬q) ⇒ r` ✅. (5) `q ⇒ r` ❌ at TTF.

items.q: Which are logically entailed by `¬p ∧ (q ⇔ ¬r)`?
items.why: Premise-rows: FFT and FTF. (1) `q ∨ r` ✅. (2) `q` ❌ at FFT. (3) `¬p ∧ ¬(q ∧ r)` ✅. (4) `¬q ⇒ ¬r` ❌ at FFT. (5) `p ∨ ¬q ∨ ¬r` ✅ (`q`, `r` are never both T).

items.q: Which are logically entailed by `(a ⇒ b) ∧ (b ⇒ c) ∧ a`?
items.why: Only one premise-row: `a = T` forces `b = T`, which forces `c = T`. (4) `b ⊕ c` = T ⊕ T = F ❌.

items.q: "The alarm goes off only if the door opens." (`g` = goes off, `d` = door opens) Which **one** option matches?
items.why: "Only if" → `g ⇒ d`, and (2) is its contrapositive.

items.q: Is `q` entailed by `(p ⇒ q) ∧ (¬p ⇒ q)`?
items.why: Either `p` or `¬p` holds, and both lead to `q`.

items.q: "I cycle unless it snows." (`c`, `s`) Which **one** option matches?
items.why: Unless = if not: `¬s ⇒ c` = `s ∨ c`.

items.q: Is `q` entailed by `(p ∧ q) ∨ (q ∧ r)`?
items.why: Both halves contain `q`, so every premise-row has `q = T`. (Factor it out: `q ∧ (p ∨ r)`.)

items.q: "The build is green just in case no test fails." (`g` = green, `f` = a test fails) Which **one** option matches?
items.why: `g ⇔ ¬f` is the same as `g ⊕ f`: exactly one of them is true.

items.q: Is `¬q` entailed by `p ⊕ q` and `p`?
items.why: `p` = T, and `⊕` needs the sides to differ, so `q` = F.

lines: Q3(b): translate each statement → rewrite → match. Watch only-if, unless, neither–nor, `¬` inside `⇔`.
Q5(b): premise-rows once, then test each option on every row.
Learn it first in L2B (translation), L3 (truth tables) and L4 (entailment).
